L3729@P107: For the second use case, numpy provides numpy.dtypes.StringDType. Below we describe how to work with both
L3730@P107: fixed-width and variable-width string arrays, how to convert between the two representations, and provide some advice
L3731@P107: for most efficiently working with string data in NumPy.
L3732@P107: 4.7.1 Fixed-width data types
L3733@P107: Before NumPy 2.0, the fixed-width numpy.str_, numpy.bytes_, and numpy.void data types were the only
L3734@P107: types available for working with strings and bytestrings in NumPy. For this reason, they are used as the default dtype for
L3735@P107: strings and bytestrings, respectively:
L3736@P107: >>> np.array(["hello", "world"])
L3737@P107: array(['hello', 'world'], dtype='<U5')
L3738@P107: Here the detected data type is '<U5', or little-endian unicode string data, with a maximum length of 5 unicode code
L3739@P107: points.
L3740@P107-108: 104 4. NumPy fundamentalsNumPy User Guide, Release 2.5.0
L3741@P108: Similarly for bytestrings:
L3742@P108: >>> np.array([b"hello", b"world"])
L3743@P108: array([b'hello', b'world'], dtype='|S5')
L3744@P108: Since this is a one-byte encoding, the byteorder is ‘|’ (not applicable), and the data type detected is a maximum 5 character
L3745@P108: bytestring.
L3746@P108: You can also use numpy.void to represent bytestrings:
L3747@P108: >>> np.array([b"hello", b"world"]).astype(np.void)
L3748@P108: array([b'\x68\x65\x6C\x6C\x6F', b'\x77\x6F\x72\x6C\x64'], dtype='|V5')
L3749@P108: This is most useful when working with byte streams that are not well represented as bytestrings, and instead are better
L3750@P108: thought of as collections of 8-bit integers.
L3751@P108: 4.7.2 Variable-width strings
L3752@P108: New in version 2.0.
L3753@P108: Note: numpy.dtypes.StringDType is a new addition to NumPy, implemented using the new support in NumPy
L3754@P108: for flexible user-defined data types and is not as extensively tested in production workflows as the older NumPy data types.
L3755@P108: Often, real-world string data does not have a predictable length. In these cases it is awkward to use fixed-width strings,
L3756@P108: since storing all the data without truncation requires knowing the length of the longest string one would like to store in
L3757@P108: the array before the array is created.
L3758@P108: To support situations like this, NumPy provides numpy.dtypes.StringDType, which stores variable-width string
L3759@P108: data in a UTF-8 encoding in a NumPy array:
L3760@P108: >>> from numpy.dtypes import StringDType
L3761@P108: >>> data = ["this is a longer string", "short string"]
L3762@P108: >>> arr = np.array(data, dtype=StringDType())
L3763@P108: >>> arr
L3764@P108: array(['this is a longer string', 'short string'], dtype=StringDType())
L3765@P108: Note that unlike fixed-width strings, StringDType is not parameterized by the maximum length of an array element,
L3766@P108: arbitrarily long or short strings can live in the same array without needing to reserve storage for padding bytes in the short
L3767@P108: strings.
L3768@P108: Also note that unlike fixed-width strings and most other NumPy data types, StringDType does not store the string
L3769@P108: data in the “main” ndarray data buffer. Instead, the array buffer is used to store metadata about where the string data
L3770@P108: are stored in memory. This difference means that code expecting the array buffer to contain string data will not function
L3771@P108: correctly, and will need to be updated to support StringDType.
L3772@P108-109: 4.7. Working with Arrays of Strings And Bytes 105NumPy User Guide, Release 2.5.0
L3773@P109: Missing data support
L3774@P109: Often string datasets are not complete, and a special label is needed to indicate that a value is missing. By default
L3775@P109: StringDType does not have any special support for missing values, besides the fact that empty strings are used to
L3776@P109: populate empty arrays:
L3777@P109: >>> np.empty(3, dtype=StringDType())
L3778@P109: array(['', '', ''], dtype=StringDType())
L3779@P109: Optionally, you can create an instance of StringDType with support for missing values by passing na_object as a
L3780@P109: keyword argument for the initializer:
L3781@P109: >>> dt = StringDType(na_object=None)
L3782@P109: >>> arr = np.array(["this array has", None, "as an entry"], dtype=dt)
L3783@P109: >>> arr
L3784@P109: array(['this array has', None, 'as an entry'],
L3785@P109: dtype=StringDType(na_object=None))
L3786@P109: >>> arr[1] is None
L3787@P109: True
L3788@P109: The na_object can be any arbitrary python object. Common choices are numpy.nan, float('nan'), None, an
L3789@P109: object specifically intended to represent missing data like pandas.NA, or a (hopefully) unique string like "__placeholder__".
L3790@P109: NumPy has special handling for NaN-like sentinels and string sentinels.
L3791@P109: NaN-like Missing Data Sentinels
L3792@P109: A NaN-like sentinel returns itself as the result of arithmetic operations. This includes the python nan float and the
L3793@P109: Pandas missing data sentinel pd.NA. NaN-like sentinels inherit these behaviors in string operations. This means that,
L3794@P109: for example, the result of addition with any other string is the sentinel:
L3795@P109: >>> dt = StringDType(na_object=np.nan)
L3796@P109: >>> arr = np.array(["hello", np.nan, "world"], dtype=dt)
L3797@P109: >>> arr + arr
L3798@P109: array(['hellohello', nan, 'worldworld'], dtype=StringDType(na_object=nan))
L3799@P109: Following the behavior of nan in float arrays, NaN-like sentinels sort to the end of the array:
L3800@P109: >>> np.sort(arr)
L3801@P109: array(['hello', 'world', nan], dtype=StringDType(na_object=nan))
L3802@P109-110: 106 4. NumPy fundamentalsNumPy User Guide, Release 2.5.0
L3803@P110: String Missing Data Sentinels
L3804@P110: A string missing data value is an instance of str or subtype of str. If such an array is passed to a string operation or
L3805@P110: a cast, “missing” entries are treated as if they have a value given by the string sentinel. Comparison operations similarly
L3806@P110: use the sentinel value directly for missing entries.
L3807@P110: Other Sentinels

L3809@P110: such a sentinel, then string operations will raise an error:
L3810@P110: >>> dt = StringDType(na_object=None)

L3812@P110: >>> np.sort(arr)

L3847@P111: The numpy.bytes_ cast is most useful for string data that is known to contain only ASCII characters, as characters
L3848@P111: outside this range cannot be represented in a single byte in the UTF-8 encoding and are rejected.
L3849@P111: Any valid unicode string can be cast to numpy.str_, although since numpy.str_ uses a 32-bit UCS4 encoding for
L3850@P111: all characters, this will often waste memory for real-world textual data that can be well-represented by a more memoryefficient encoding.
L3851@P111: Additionally, any valid unicode string can be cast to numpy.void, storing the UTF-8 bytes directly in the output array:
L3852@P111: >>> arr = np.array(["hello", "world"], dtype=StringDType())
L3853@P111: >>> arr.astype("V5")
L3854@P111: array([b'\x68\x65\x6C\x6C\x6F', b'\x77\x6F\x72\x6C\x64'], dtype='|V5')
L3855@P111: Care must be taken to ensure that the output array has enough space for the UTF-8 bytes in the string, since the size of a
L3856@P111: UTF-8 bytestream in bytes is not necessarily the same as the number of characters in the string.
L3857@P111: 4.8 Structured arrays
L3858@P111: 4.8.1 Introduction
L3859@P111: Structured arrays are ndarrays whose datatype is a composition of simpler datatypes organized as a sequence of named
L3860@P111: fields. For example,
L3861@P111: >>> x = np.array([('Rex', 9, 81.0), ('Fido', 3, 27.0)],
L3862@P111: ... dtype=[('name', 'U10'), ('age', 'i4'), ('weight', 'f4')])
L3863@P111: >>> x
L3864@P111: array([('Rex', 9, 81.), ('Fido', 3, 27.)],
L3865@P111: dtype=[('name', '<U10'), ('age', '<i4'), ('weight', '<f4')])
L3866@P111: Here x is a one-dimensional array of length two whose datatype is a structure with three fields: 1. A string of length 10
L3867@P111: or less named ‘name’, 2. a 32-bit integer named ‘age’, and 3. a 32-bit float named ‘weight’.
L3868@P111: If you index x at position 1 you get a structure:
L3869@P111: >>> x[1]
L3870@P111: np.void(('Fido', 3, 27.0), dtype=[('name', '<U10'), ('age', '<i4'), ('weight', '<f4
L3871@P111: ,→')])
L3872@P111: You can access and modify individual fields of a structured array by indexing with the field name:
L3873@P111: >>> x['age']
L3874@P111: array([9, 3], dtype=int32)
L3875@P111: >>> x['age'] = 5
L3876@P111: >>> x
L3877@P111: array([('Rex', 5, 81.), ('Fido', 5, 27.)],
L3878@P111: dtype=[('name', '<U10'), ('age', '<i4'), ('weight', '<f4')])
L3879@P111: Structured datatypes are designed to be able to mimic ‘structs’ in the C language, and share a similar memory layout. They
L3880@P111: are meant for interfacing with C code and for low-level manipulation of structured buffers, for example for interpreting
L3881@P111: binary blobs. For these purposes they support specialized features such as subarrays, nested datatypes, and unions, and
L3882@P111: allow control over the memory layout of the structure.
L3883@P111-112: 108 4. NumPy fundamentalsNumPy User Guide, Release 2.5.0
L3884@P112: Users looking to manipulate tabular data, such as stored in csv files, may find other pydata projects more suitable, such as
L3885@P112: xarray, pandas, or DataArray. These provide a high-level interface for tabular data analysis and are better optimized for
L3886@P112: that use. For instance, the C-struct-like memory layout of structured arrays in numpy can lead to poor cache behavior in
L3887@P112: comparison.
L3888@P112: 4.8.2 Structured datatypes
L3889@P112: A structured datatype can be thought of as a sequence of bytes of a certain length (the structure’s itemsize) which is
L3890@P112: interpreted as a collection of fields. Each field has a name, a datatype, and a byte offset within the structure. The datatype
L3891@P112: of a field may be any numpy datatype including other structured datatypes, and it may also be a subarray data type which
L3892@P112: behaves like an ndarray of a specified shape. The offsets of the fields are arbitrary, and fields may even overlap. These
L3893@P112: offsets are usually determined automatically by numpy, but can also be specified.

L14565@P394: – numpy.matvec - matrix-vector product, treating the arguments as stacks of matrices and column vectors,
L14566@P394: respectively.

L14568@P394: respectively. For complex vectors, the conjugate is taken.

L14571@P394: numpy.vecdot and numpy.vecmat do take the conjugate for complex vectors on the left-hand side (which
L14572@P394: are taken to be the ones that are transposed, following the physics convention).
